source.title: Effective Learning Rate Governs Loss Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
source.authors: Zi-Han Liu; Rui-Heng Zheng; Shaobo Zhang; Chang-Xin Tian; Kun-Long Chen; Zhi-Qiang Zhang; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines the predictive-law claim by testing whether functional scaling-law predictions transfer across norm-control regimes when parameterized by learning rate versus effective learning rate. It does not test the original parameter/token/compute power laws.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling-law results concern prediction of training-loss trajectories for one 124M language model across schedules and norm-control regimes, not loss scaling with model parameters, tokens, or compute. The paper also reports ELR-collapse results, but those do not measure the behaviors named by the claim versions. No rows are included for those results.
record.test_reason: The study is about effective-learning-rate (ELR) collapse of loss trajectories. Its scaling-law section uses the functional scaling law (FSL) of Li et al. as a tool to model a single 124M model's training-loss curve under different LR schedules. It then compares its own ELR-parameterized variant (elr-FSL) against the LR-parameterized original (lr-FSL). There is no loss scaling with parameters, tokens or compute, no compute-optimal fit, no architecture-shape sweep and no downstream measure. The rows measure the study's own method against a comparator for a different construct: within-run loss dynamics under a schedule. They are not the fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits that V7 names.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors' main conclusion is ELR collapse: when ELR schedules are matched, loss trajectories collapse to within a few ×10^-3, across optimizers, architectures (100M–1B), datasets and a ViT. The precision depends on QK-Norm, learnable RMSNorm gains and slow LR–norm variation. Weight decay and Hyperball act mainly through the ELR they induce. Swapping LR for ELR also lets a fitted FSL transfer to unseen Hyperball runs (about 12x lower error) and explains delayed acceleration. The record's paraphrase covers only the FSL-transfer part.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the parameter/token/compute power-law fits or compute-optimal allocation methods of the original sources. It evaluates a functional scaling law for loss trajectories, comparing LR and ELR as its input coordinate.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported FSL prediction accuracy depends on whether trajectories are parameterized by LR or ELR and on the norm-control regime: the largest difference is on held-out Hyperball runs, which were absent from fitting.

fits_no_version.finding: A functional scaling law for loss trajectories over training, fitted on non-Hyperball runs of Llama-124M/FineWeb, predicts unseen Hyperball runs far better when driven by ELR (mean RMSE 0.0212) than by LR (0.2508). ELR also helps on held-out ID schedules (0.0133 vs 0.0239). lr-FSL is better on one fitting run (0.0069 vs 0.0138).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Schedule-aware loss-trajectory laws (FSL) transfer across norm-control regimes only when parameterized by effective learning rate rather than raw learning rate.

record.problems: The scaling-law transfer experiment uses one model size, 124M, and one dataset, FineWeb; it does not assess transfer across model sizes, token budgets, or compute budgets. Reported RMSE values have no uncertainty estimates. The paper states that matched training-loss trajectories need not imply matched downstream performance.

untested.parts: Power-law dependence of held-out loss on parameters, tokens or compute. All FSL runs use one 124M model and fixed steps.
Extrapolation from small to much larger runs. The transfer tested is across LR schedules and norm-control methods at a fixed scale.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters versus tokens.
Effect of depth or width at fixed parameter count on loss. The normalization ablations measure collapse error, not loss scaling.
Power-law form in other modalities or regimes. The ViT experiment measures ELR collapse error only.
Downstream predictability. The authors state that matched loss need not imply matched downstream performance.
Dependence of fitted exponents or the compute-optimal split on setup or fitting choices, disagreement between published laws, and bending away from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 link is a stretch. V7 concerns how exponents and compute-optimal splits depend on setup and fitting choices across published laws. This study varies only the input coordinate of a within-run schedule law, at one model size, and compares its own proposed variant with the original. That makes it a method comparison (T4), not a test. There is an internal inconsistency: the main text says 11.83x and the abstract and caption say 12.9x; these are aggregate ratio versus mean of per-run ratios. No uncertainty is reported on the RMSEs. The paper is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law dependence of held-out pretraining loss on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger; the tested FSL transfer is across schedules and norm-control regimes at the same model scale.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and tokens, and how either scales with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes. The ViT experiment tests ELR trajectory collapse, not power-law loss scaling.
Downstream-task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study tests whether changing the FSL input coordinate (LR versus ELR) changes loss-trajectory prediction across norm-control settings. It does not test fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, disagreement between the Kaplan and Hoffmann laws, or bending away from a single power law.
